sources.title: NGSS MS-LS4-2: Apply scientific ideas to construct an explanation for the anatomical similarities and differences among modern organisms and between modern and fossil organisms to infer evolutionary relationships

legend.name: Wrist and hand
legend.meaning: Drawn as lines; many small bones

steps.title: Upper arm
steps.instruction: Trace the upper arm bone in all four limbs.

note.text: A human arm, a dog's front leg, a bird's wing and a whale's flipper all start with one upper bone.

steps.title: Forearm
steps.instruction: Trace the pair of forearm bones in each limb.

note.text: Next come two forearm bones, side by side, in all four.

steps.title: Hand
steps.instruction: Draw the hand bones in each limb.

note.text: Then come wrist and hand bones: long fingers in the flipper, few and fused in the wing.

steps.title: Color
steps.instruction: Color the matching bones the same color in every limb.

steps.title: Same plan
steps.question: These limbs do very different jobs. Why do they have the same layout of bones?

options.text: They were inherited from a common ancestor
options.feedback: Yes. Parts with the same basic structure from a shared ancestor are called homologous structures.

options.text: They all do the same job
options.feedback: They don't: grabbing, running, flying, swimming. The layout comes from a shared ancestor.
The same bones in the same order in so many animals points to a common ancestor.

options.text: Bones can only grow one way
options.feedback: Bones vary hugely. These match because of shared ancestry.

steps.title: Differences
steps.instruction: Look at the shapes and sizes.
steps.question: Why are the bones different shapes and sizes in each animal?

options.text: Over time, evolution changed them to suit each animal's way of life
options.feedback: Right. The layout stayed the same, but shapes and sizes changed for swimming, flying, running or grabbing.
The shared layout shows a common ancestor. The shapes changed over time.

options.text: Each animal grows its bones however it likes
options.feedback: Bone shapes are inherited. They changed over many generations.
Compare the flipper's short upper bone with the human's long one.

steps.title: Infer
steps.question: Whales live in water like fish. What do their flipper bones suggest?

options.text: Whales are more closely related to land mammals than to fish
options.feedback: Yes. Their flippers hide the same arm bones as a human or dog, inherited from mammal ancestors.

options.text: Whales are a kind of fish
options.feedback: Their limb bones match mammals' arms, not fish fins. Whales are mammals.
Every species has ancestors. The bones point to land-mammal relatives.
Homologous bones are strong evidence of shared ancestry.
